findings.title: Options-object calls reject queued promises by default despite rejectOnClear defaulting to false
findings.cause: The options destructuring changed the fallback to `rejectOnClear = true`, so `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` enables abort rejection even when callers did not opt in.
findings.impact: A documented default changes only for options-object users: pending promises that used to be silently discarded/remain pending after `clearQueue()` now reject with AbortError, which can break Promise.all flows and surface unexpected errors during teardown.
findings.evidence: readme.md documents `rejectOnClear` default as false and says pending promises reject when the option is enabled. index.d.ts also documents Default: false. Current index.js line 7 defaults the option to true.
findings.reproduction_or_test: In-memory runtime probe of current index.js: create `const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1})`, queue one never-settling task and one pending task, await a microtask, call `limit.clearQueue()`, then race the pending promise against a timeout. Observed output: `default-clearQueue: rejected:AbortError`; expected default behavior is not to reject unless `rejectOnClear: true` is supplied.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values are accepted at runtime
findings.cause: The runtime type check is gated by `rejectOnClear &&`, so only truthy non-booleans throw and falsy invalid values bypass validation.
findings.impact: Invalid option values such as `0`, empty string, or `null` are silently accepted even though the public type and original runtime contract require a boolean. This can hide caller configuration bugs and diverges from TypeScript expectations for JavaScript users.
findings.evidence: index.d.ts defines `readonly rejectOnClear?: boolean`, and index.test-d.ts has `expectError(pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 'nope'}))`. The original HEAD implementation checked `typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean'` unconditionally after defaulting.
findings.reproduction_or_test: In-memory runtime probe of current index.js: `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0})`, `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: ""})`, and `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: null})` all printed `accepted`; `rejectOnClear: "no"` threw. Expected all non-boolean supplied values to throw.

findings.title: limitFunction drops every caller argument
findings.cause: The wrapper returned by `limitFunction` no longer accepts rest arguments and invokes `function_()` with no arguments.
findings.impact: Any limited function that depends on parameters receives `undefined` values. This breaks the exported TypeScript signature, the recipes.md URL example, and benchmark.js limitFunction scenario that maps delays and indexes into the limited function.
findings.evidence: index.d.ts declares `limitFunction<Arguments...>(function_): (...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`. recipes.md calls `limitedFetchUrl(url)`. benchmark.js calls `limitedTask(delay, i)`. Current index.js returns `() => limit(() => function_())`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: In-memory runtime probe of current index.js: `const limited = limitFunction((a, b) => [a, b], {concurrency: 1}); await limited("x", "y")` produced `[null,null]` when JSON stringified, meaning both arguments were `undefined`; expected `["x","y"]`.

findings.title: limit.map omits the index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call conditionally passes the index only when `Array.isArray(iterable)` is true; Set, generator, and iterator inputs receive `undefined` instead.
findings.impact: The documented `limit.map` contract is broken for supported iterable inputs. Callers using Set or iterator inputs with index-aware mapping get incorrect results even though the type signature guarantees `index: number`.
findings.evidence: readme.md says the mapper receives item value and index and is equivalent to `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index))`. index.d.ts repeats this contract and tests include non-array iterables, though current tests do not assert index for them.
findings.reproduction_or_test: In-memory runtime probe of current index.js: `await pLimit(2).map(new Set(["a", "b"]), (value, index) => `${value}:${index}`)` produced `["a:undefined","b:undefined"]`; expected `["a:0","b:1"]`.

findings.title: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY is no longer accepted as a concurrency limit
findings.cause: The validator now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency)` and removed the explicit `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` allowance present in HEAD.
findings.impact: Existing users who use Infinity to disable limiting while preserving the p-limit API now get a TypeError. This is a compatibility regression from the repository baseline and from the broad `number` concurrency surface.
findings.evidence: git show HEAD:index.js lines 123-125 accepted `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`; current index.js line 128 accepts only positive integers.
findings.reproduction_or_test: In-memory runtime probe of current index.js: `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)` printed `infinity-threw: Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up`; expected construction to succeed as in HEAD.
